g.text: handle() may do anything. apply() must be pure. The types enforce it.
A single combined process(command) would leave nothing preventing an apply-time clock read - a bug silent until an audit.
The most important boundary in the design
interface CommandHandler
handle(cmd, state: StateView) -> Result<List<Event>, Rejection>
read-only StateView. May call a fraud service,
read the clock, generate a UUID. Runs ONCE.
interface EventApplier
apply(state: MutableState, event) -> void
MutableState. A PURE function: no clock, no I/O,
no randomness. Runs on EVERY replay.
Different state TYPES, deliberately: apply() has no handle on which to call an external service, and no legitimate reason to
reach for now(). The compiler helps. Projection.rebuild() is likewise on the interface as a first-class operation rather than
an admin script - it is what makes a projection bug retroactively fixable, so every author must think about whether theirs
can actually be rebuilt.
Four optimizations, in order of impact - 1,000 TPS to ~100,000
1. sequential append,
not random update
~150 MB/s vs ~0.6 MB/s. At 200 bytes/event
that is 750,000 events/sec theoretical, so
THE DISK STOPS BEING THE BOTTLENECK - which
tells you to optimize CPU and network next.
2. state in memory,
not on disk
100M accounts x 64 bytes = 6.4 GB per
partition. No disk read to validate.
Only safe because state is DERIVABLE - a
conventional design cannot do this.
3. mmap the event file
An append becomes a memcpy: 100k syscalls/sec
removed. Acceptable ONLY because durability
comes from Raft replication rather than a
local fsync.
4. ONE thread,
pinned to one core
No locks, no context switches, hot cache -
and SERIAL EXECUTION BECOMES THE CONCURRENCY
CONTROL. Multi-core capacity comes from many
partitions per machine.
The reframe worth leading with: this is not a sharding problem, it is a 'make one node fast enough that you barely need to
shard' problem. 2,000 nodes becomes 20 partitions - 60 machines at RF 3.
Concurrency: the design ELIMINATES the intra-process race rather than guarding it
Needs no lock at all
two debits on one account the single-threaded leader serializes them; the
second validates against updated state
balance reads served from projections - separate processes
log appends one writer per partition by construction
cross-partition transfers TC/C's committed local transactions replace
the distributed lock a 2PC design would need
Needs coordination
the command queue a lock-free ring buffer: many network threads
produce, one application thread consumes
PhaseStatus transitions compare-and-set, so two recovery workers
racing on one transfer resolve to one winner
Raft internals leader election and log replication
apply() runs only AFTER raft.propose() commits. Applying before commit would let the leader's in-memory state reflect an event
that a subsequent election discards - the same hazard the message queue's high watermark prevents. State must never run ahead
of the committed log.
Patterns, named
Event Sourcing state as a fold over an immutable log
CQRS separate write model and read projections
State Machine Replication Raft replicates the LOG, and every replica applies it deterministically to reach identical
state - so the determinism rule is not fussiness, it is what makes SMR sound
Compensating Transaction TC/C's Cancel phase
Tombstone the out-of-order cancel flag: a marker for an operation that has not arrived yet
Single-threaded event loop one thread, lock-free, pinned
